Tittabawassee Ojibwe communities

Also find this entry through: Tittabawassee River communities

Explore the Tittabawassee River communities through Michigan treaty records, an attributed nineteenth-century account, and Saginaw Chippewa community sources. This regional reading route is placed in Ojibwe context and does not identify a separate present-day tribal government.

A historical/regional river-community reading route, not a separately established present government or an exclusive descent claim.

  1. History — Ziibiwing Center

    Begin with the Tribe-published account that supplies present Saginaw Chippewa context.

  2. Treaty with the Chippewa, September 24, 1819 (7 Stat. 203)

    Read the dated1819 instrument and its named river tracts within the recorded transcription scope.

  3. History of the Ottawa and Chippewa Indians of Michigan (1887), selected Tittabawassee passage

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

A river-community name and its scope

This is a historical and regional reading route for Indigenous communities associated with the Tittabawassee River in Michigan’s Saginaw watershed. It is not the name of a separate contemporary government established by this review. The Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe describes itself through three Ojibway bands: Saginaw, Black River and Swan Creek. That broader community history should not be reduced to a fourth band called Tittabawassee, or an exclusive descent claim for every river settlement.

Read the sources [1] Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan, Ziibiwing Center [5] Andrew J. Blackbird; University of Wisconsin–Madison-hosted transcription

02

The river and historical place-names

The 1819 treaty names Little Forks and Black Bird’s town on the river printed as Tetabawasink. The January 1837 text uses Tetabwasing. Clarke Historical Library’s Houghton exhibit connects Black Bird Reservation and the 1819 treaty with the Tittabawassee–Chippewa river landscape near Midland. These records help orient the reading, but do not supply a complete settlement inventory or justify drawing precise community boundaries.

Read the sources [2] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; primary treaty transcription [3] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; primary treaty transcription [9] Clarke Historical Library, Central Michigan University

03

Reading the 1819 and January 1837 treaties

The September 24, 1819 agreement identifies Chippewa parties and reserves two 6,000-acre tracts at Little Forks and Black Bird’s town. The January 14, 1837 agreement, made at Detroit with Saganaw/Chippewa parties, lists those tracts among the lands ceded and prescribes relocation. Treaty wording is evidence of the instrument and its terms; individual experiences, enforcement and later rights require separate study.

Read the sources [2] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; primary treaty transcription [3] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; primary treaty transcription

04

Why the December 1837 supplement matters

The December 20 agreement at Flint River modifies the January treaty, including relocation and financial provisions. The two supplied 1837 links therefore represent different, related Michigan agreements. Their listed proclamation date in 1838 should not replace their treaty dates. A proposed destination does not demonstrate that all local people relocated or that their communities disappeared.

Read the sources [3] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; primary treaty transcription [4] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; primary treaty transcription

05

An attributed account of river travel

In his 1887 book, Andrew J. Blackbird recalls a winter journey seeking support for Native citizenship. He describes following the frozen Tittabawassee, finding one camp deserted and receiving food at another where women and children remained while men hunted. This is his personal recollection of a particular encounter. He does not name every host or establish a genealogy for the camps, so the episode should not become a universal description of river life.

Read the sources [5] Andrew J. Blackbird; University of Wisconsin–Madison-hosted transcription

06

Continuing communities, education and watershed care

The Ziibiwing Center shares the Saginaw Chippewa Tribe’s account of continuing community institutions. A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service restoration story, framed around the 2020 settlement, describes the Tribe’s cultural use of wetlands and planned habitat work in the wider Saginaw Bay area. The Tribal College’s history offers a further community-led educational route. These sources concern particular institutions and projects, rather than one unchanging river community or a claim that planned restoration is complete.

Read the sources [1] Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan, Ziibiwing Center [6] U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service [8] Saginaw Chippewa Tribal College

07

Language and further reading

Ojibwe language resources provide broader context, but their regional coverage matters. The Ojibwe People’s Dictionary identifies its main variety as Central Southwestern Ojibwe from Minnesota, Wisconsin and border-lakes communities. It should not be treated as a record of historical Tittabawassee pronunciation. The owner-supplied study and all 19 contributed links are retained below; only the sources with explicit inspection notes have been checked for this guide.

Read the sources [7] Ojibwe People’s Dictionary, University of Minnesota

History — Ziibiwing Center ↗

The Tribe’s own historical account identifies its three Ojibway bands and describes reservation history, reorganization and the cultural center. It supplies present-community context, not an exclusive descent chart for river settlements.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete visible chronology and prose read, especially the three-band statement and reservation/reorganization paragraphs. Ancient chronology, numerical land-loss claims and broad legal assertions are not independently corroborated here.
